opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the right way to approach this is to look at what's actually driven progress historically and then ask whether the underlying dynamics are likely to change.

When you look at the empirical record, at least for things like language models and computer vision, you can try to decompose improvements in performance into two buckets. One is the growth in effective compute that comes from simply throwing more physical compute at training runs: more chips, better chips, bigger budgets. The other is algorithmic progress: better architectures, better training recipes, better data, which lets you reach the same performance with less compute. When people have done this kind of decomposition, you tend to find that both are contributing on the same order of magnitude. Physical compute for frontier training runs has been growing very fast, something like four or five times per year, and algorithmic efficiency has also been improving at a rate where the compute needed to hit a fixed level of performance falls by a large factor each year. These are in the same ballpark, maybe with compute scaling having a somewhat larger share recently.

But I think there's a deeper reason to expect rough parity, beyond just the historical accident of the numbers lining up. The two are complements, not substitutes. A lot of algorithmic progress is itself driven by compute. Researchers discover improvements by running experiments, and the number and scale of experiments you can run depends on how much compute you have. Many innovations, like certain architectural tweaks or training techniques, only show their value at scale, so you can't even find them without large amounts of hardware. So in a sense, software progress is partly downstream of hardware progress. If hardware stalled, I'd expect algorithmic progress to slow substantially too, and vice versa: without good algorithms, the returns to scaling up hardware would be much weaker.

When you have two inputs that are strongly complementary like that, it's natural for them to grow together and contribute comparably. The bottleneck shifts to whichever one is lagging, which tends to pull them back into balance. You don't really get a world where one races ahead indefinitely while the other stays flat.

There's also an economic argument. Labs are allocating budgets between buying compute and paying researchers and engineers. If one of those were giving a much higher marginal return, you'd expect resources to flow toward it until returns roughly equalized. That kind of optimization pressure also pushes toward both mattering a similar amount at the margin.

Now, I'd add caveats. The decomposition is genuinely hard to do well. Measuring algorithmic progress is noisy, and it's tricky to separate out things like data quality improvements, or gains that only appear at particular scales. And there are scenarios where the balance could shift. For instance, if AI systems themselves start automating a lot of AI research, you could see software progress accelerate in a way that's less tied to human researcher headcount, though even then it would still need lots of compute to run those automated researchers and their experiments. So I wouldn't say it's a law of nature that they're exactly equal, but I think "same order of magnitude, and tightly coupled" is a pretty robust expectation.

r001.rationale: The response cites estimates of hardware and algorithmic contributions in language models and computer vision, plus complementarity and economic arguments. It does not mention a recurring roughly equal split in other computer science domains as evidence.

fable-5.1.text:
So this comes from work we did at Epoch looking at where the gains in AI capabilities have actually come from. We tried to decompose progress into a compute component and an algorithmic component, and when you do that carefully across a range of domains, you find they've been contributing roughly comparable amounts.

The intuition is something like this. Compute, the physical hardware side, has been growing very fast. For frontier training runs we estimate something like a four to five times increase per year over the past decade or so. That's a combination of hardware getting more cost-effective, which is a Moore's-law-type effect, and labs simply spending more money, which has been the bigger driver recently.

But algorithms have also improved a great deal. In language modeling, for example, our estimate is that the compute needed to reach a fixed level of performance halves roughly every eight months. So that's also several-fold improvement per year in effective compute. When you put those on the same scale, physical compute growth and algorithmic efficiency gains end up in the same ballpark.

Now, why would you expect them to be roughly balanced rather than one dominating? Part of it is just empirical, that's what we observe. But there's also a structural argument. If you think of a lab as allocating resources between buying more compute and doing research that improves algorithms, a well-run lab will push on both until the marginal returns are roughly equalized. If software were far cheaper to improve than hardware, you'd expect labs to shift effort there until it stopped being cheap, and vice versa. So you get something like an equilibrium where both inputs matter comparably.

The other thing I'd say is that the two aren't really independent. A lot of what we call algorithmic progress is actually about using compute better, scaling laws, better data mixes, more efficient architectures. Those insights are unlocked by having more compute to experiment with. So it's not quite hardware versus software, it's more that both are inputs into the same production process, and historically they've scaled together.

I should be clear that there's real uncertainty in these estimates. Decomposing progress like this is hard, and the numbers vary across domains. But the broad picture, that neither one is a rounding error, seems robust. If anything, I'd expect the software side to become more important as compute spending becomes harder to scale and as AI itself starts contributing to AI research.

r001.rationale: The response cites estimates of comparable compute and algorithmic contributions within AI, but does not use a recurring hardware/software split in other computer science domains as evidence.

astra-6.text:
I think of that as a rough expectation rather than a precise prediction. Hardware and software are two ways of getting more useful computation: you can build faster chips and use more of them, or you can develop algorithms that achieve the same performance with less compute.

They’re also complementary. Better hardware makes it possible to experiment with new algorithms, and better algorithms make the hardware more valuable. If one were contributing much less, you might expect there to be relatively attractive opportunities to invest in improving it.

That doesn’t imply an exact fifty-fifty split. There’s no law that says their contributions must be equal, and software progress is particularly difficult to measure. But I’d put substantial weight on both, rather than assume that future progress will come overwhelmingly from just one.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses hardware and software as complementary sources of AI progress, but does not cite recurring findings from other computer science domains as evidence for expecting a similar split.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic intuition is that hardware and software are two complementary ways of getting more capability out of a given budget. You can build faster chips and larger clusters, or you can improve the algorithms so that you need less computation to achieve the same result.

If one of those routes were consistently much more productive than the other, you’d expect investment and research effort to shift toward it. And as you put more effort into that route, you’d tend to encounter diminishing returns. So there’s a reason to expect the contributions to be of a similar order of magnitude, although that doesn’t imply an exact fifty-fifty split.

There’s also some empirical support for this: algorithmic improvements have substantially reduced the compute required to achieve a given level of performance, at rates that are comparable to improvements in hardware. So I’d treat roughly equal contributions as a reasonable starting point, rather than a particularly precise prediction.
